claim: In the tested peg-in-hole settings, model-free PPO policies using sparse asymmetric Cartesian impedance/admittance matrices achieved higher reported insertion success than diagonal or symmetric-matrix alternatives, while retaining high success under selected simulated and zero-shot real-world variants.
claim_locator: Full-text packet: simulation small-peg insertion comparisons
Full-text packet: space-invariant versus space-dependent policy comparison
Full-text packet: UR5e zero-shot sim-to-real experiments
epistemic_status: Author-reported empirical evidence with statistical comparisons; mechanism interpretation is plausible but task-bounded, and no formal stability or passivity guarantee is supplied.
problem_and_setting: Learning contact-responsive Cartesian impedance/admittance policies for peg-in-hole insertion when the hole location is estimated imperfectly. Experiments include simulated small-peg insertion and zero-shot transfer to a UR5e robot with force/torque sensing, plus tested rigid and semi-flexible insertion variants.
method_or_mechanism: A model-free PPO policy conditions Cartesian inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices on the estimated hole location while retaining a minimum-jerk nominal trajectory and modifying motion after contact. Compared policy action structures are diagonal, non-diagonal symmetric, and asymmetric stiffness/damping matrices. Inertia remains diagonal positive definite. Asymmetric matrices are constrained by requiring their symmetric part to be positive definite, and only four off-diagonal couplings are enabled. The antisymmetric or curl component is intended to map force/torque along one axis into corrective motion along another.
content_summary: The paper reports that asymmetric impedance policies outperform diagonal and symmetric alternatives in simulated small-peg insertion. Best asymmetric policies reach 98.5% success, whereas diagonal policies range from 70% to 94.5% with a 78% mean and symmetric policies range from 80% to 97% with a 90% mean. Wilcoxon comparisons favor asymmetric policies over diagonal policies at p=.004 and over symmetric policies at p=.01. A space-invariant mean policy retains 98% success versus 98.5% for the space-dependent policy. Zero-shot transfer to a UR5e yields 84% basic-task success, below the 98.5% simulation result; reported rigid-task variants include 79%, 94%, and 84% success. Semi-flexible wire/connector tasks exceed 80% success, compared with below 55% for PD control, with non-overlapping confidence intervals in some comparisons. The first five real-world conditions use 200 trials each and the final two use 100 each.
synthesis_role: Provides comparative empirical evidence that deliberately structured asymmetric impedance couplings can improve contact-rich insertion and may transfer from simulation to hardware, while also defining important limits on generality and formal safety claims.
development_link: Supports developing impedance-policy parameterizations that expose sparse cross-axis antisymmetric couplings while enforcing positive definiteness of the symmetric component; motivates evaluating such policies against diagonal and symmetric baselines in both simulation and hardware.

evidence.finding: Basic real-world success was 84%, below the reported 98.5% simulation success; rigid variants reportedly achieved 79%, 94%, and 84%.
Learned policies reportedly exceeded 80% success, while PD control remained below 55%; some comparisons had non-overlapping confidence intervals.
Only four off-diagonal couplings were allowed; inertia was diagonal positive definite, and learned asymmetric matrices were checked by requiring a positive-definite symmetric part.

boundary_conditions: Policies use task-specific sparse matrix structures with only four permitted off-diagonal couplings.
The approach depends on contact force/torque sensing and an estimated hole location.
Training and policy optimization are tied to a PPO-based simulation design.
Training centers on a small-peg insertion task.
Hardware generalization is demonstrated only for the tested rigid and semi-flexible variants.
No formal closed-loop stability or passivity proof is supplied.
Real-world success remains below the best simulation result in the basic transfer condition.
The first five real conditions use 200 trials each and the final two use 100 each.
assumptions: Positive definiteness of the asymmetric matrix's symmetric part is treated as an adequate admissibility check for the learned matrix parameterization.
The retained minimum-jerk trajectory provides a suitable nominal approach before contact-driven corrections.
Simulation contact dynamics and sensing are sufficiently representative to support zero-shot hardware transfer.
Reported success rates and statistical comparisons are valid for the stated protocols.

reported: Basic zero-shot UR5e success decreased to 84% from 98.5% in simulation.
Some tested rigid real-world variants achieved only 79% or 84% success.
Diagonal and symmetric action structures produced lower reported mean or best-case simulation success than the asymmetric structure.
PD control achieved below 55% success on the tested semi-flexible tasks.
inferred: Because only sparse, task-selected couplings were tested, performance may depend on prior structural choices and may not extend to arbitrary contact tasks.
Without a formal stability or passivity analysis, positive definiteness of the symmetric component alone does not establish closed-loop safety under all interactions.
The zero-shot simulation-to-real performance gap suggests sensitivity to unmodeled hardware, sensing, or contact-dynamics differences.
Near-equivalent success of space-invariant and space-dependent policies suggests spatial conditioning may contribute little in the tested setting.

verification_status: Verified only against the Controller-supplied full-text packet; numerical results, statistical claims, novelty, and comparative conclusions remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.
